clue.text: Bird on a plate - but he flew in the past

indicators.note: in an across clue one part sitting on another is placed after it, so the bird comes last

blocks.note: the L-plate shown by a learner driver

explanation.surface: A chicken served up on a dish, which once had wings of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: John Alcock piloted the first non-stop transatlantic flight in 1919 with Arthur Brown. An L-plate is the red L a British learner driver must display.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcock was the pioneering aviator of the Alcock and Brown Atlantic crossing, long ago.

clue.text: Handout for a defunct railway

blocks.note: the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, merged away in 1948

explanation.surface: A subsidy paid out to a railway company that no longer runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The LMS was one of Britain's big four railway companies before nationalisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are charitable gifts of money or food given freely to poor people.

clue.text: Monster - we must have him taken into care somehow

indicators.note: done somehow means done in some unspecified way, so the word before it is rearranged
something taken into a place is put inside it, so one word goes within the other

explanation.surface: A frightening man must be put into residential care by some means.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'him' as the monster; really it is just three letters slotted into a scrambled word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chimera of Greek myth was a fire-breathing beast, part lion, goat and serpent.

clue.text: False direction gets one lost in town

indicators.note: a false version is not the true one, so the letters appear in a wrong order
something lost is no longer there, so that piece is removed

explanation.surface: Wrong directions make a visitor lose their way in a town.
explanation.walkthrough: Crediton is a small market town in Devon, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Crediton is an example of a town, a market settlement near Exeter in Devon.

clue.text: Ambitious worker goes to Paris for a change

indicators.note: doing something for a change means doing it differently, so the city's letters are reordered

blocks.note: the worker ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: A go-getting employee heads off to Paris to try something new.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirant as an adjective describes someone aspiring or striving for advancement or success.

clue.text: Blow one's top in it?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a gale from a particular quarter, or the waterproof hat you wear on your head out in it

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a wind (a blow) and, as sou'wester, the oilskin hat (one's top) worn in such weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind from the south-west is a blow, and the sailor's waterproof hat shares the name.

clue.text: Where tenants may be up creeks

blocks.note: first meaning: split as two words, occupying rented properties
second meaning: narrow arms of the sea or a river

explanation.surface: Renters may find themselves up the creek without a paddle.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as IN LETS: tenants live in lets, properties let to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Inlets are small bays or narrow water channels running into the land, much like creeks.

clue.text: Swiss banker takes on an extra name

indicators.note: the banker takes on the following words by being wrapped in them

blocks.note: taken as written, split around the other piece
the gnomes of Zurich, a nickname for Swiss financiers

explanation.surface: A Zurich financier adopts a further name.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gnomes of Zurich was a 1960s British jibe at Swiss bankers.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnomen was a fourth name a Roman earned, so in general an additional name or epithet.

clue.text: Numbers reject Euro to delay entry

indicators.note: whatever is rejected is thrown out, so that letter goes from the number

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European or euro
to hold up or put off

explanation.surface: Sums of money reject the single currency to delay a nation joining.
explanation.definitionFit: A threshold is the sill of a doorway, hence the point of entry or beginning.

clue.text: Fellows need help in getting her

indicators.note: one word placed in another sits inside it

explanation.surface: Men require assistance in winning a woman's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word 'her', a young woman who is the object of the fellows' pursuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden is a girl or young unmarried woman, the female figure referred to by her.

clue.text: Name a ship after Joyce, perhaps

blocks.note: to dub is to name or title

explanation.surface: A vessel is to be named in honour of the writer James Joyce.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyce was born in Dublin and wrote the story collection Dubliners.
explanation.definitionFit: James Joyce was a native of Ireland's capital city, an example of one born there.

clue.text: Where Rupert is too conservative?

blocks.note: first meaning: Rupert Murdoch owns The Times newspaper, so he stands at the back of it
second meaning: old-fashioned, out of date

explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Murdoch bought The Times of London in 1981; the proprietor is literally the man behind the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stuck in outdated ways and resisting modern ideas is said to be out of touch with current fashion.

clue.text: Saturnalia could be gory

blocks.note: surface reading: a Roman festival of excess might turn bloody
setter's reading: the answer's second word is that four-letter word made tipsy, its letters staggering about

explanation.walkthrough: The answer's first word acts like an anagram signal on its second, which is a jumble of the word gory.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman Saturnalia was a feast of riotous revelry, so the word now means any wild, debauched party.

clue.text: He maintains frequency by rescheduling one up train

indicators.note: rescheduling a train timetable changes its order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A railway manager keeps services frequent by retiming a London-bound train.
explanation.walkthrough: An up train is one heading to London in British railway usage, which strengthens the railway picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano tuner adjusts strings so each note sounds at its correct pitch, keeping the instrument in tune.

clue.text: Lead on a string

blocks.note: surface reading: to string someone along, or a dog's leash
setter's reading: the heavy metal, as a weight hanging on a cord

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin for lead is plumbum, and a builder's weight on a cord shows the true vertical.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumb line is a cord with a lead weight used to check that walls stand vertical.

clue.text: A French officer is unusual

blocks.note: the French masculine word for a

explanation.surface: A Gallic army officer strikes people as strange.
explanation.walkthrough: Unco is a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, unco means strange, remarkable or uncommon, the dialect form of uncouth.

clue.text: A club to take up church teaching?  It's for killing

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: Religious Instruction, the old name for the school subject

explanation.surface: Someone takes a cudgel to Sunday school lessons, and the result is lethal.
explanation.walkthrough: RI, religious instruction, was the British school subject now called RE.
explanation.definitionFit: An abattoir is a slaughterhouse, the building where animals are killed for meat.

clue.text: Drive is something in our genes

indicators.note: something in the words that follow is a run of letters lying within them

explanation.surface: Ambition is something we inherit genetically.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive and urge both mean a strong inner impulse or motivation to act.

clue.text: This with means to support

blocks.note: surface reading: something paired with financial means
setter's reading: put the answer before the word with and the phrase means to back someone

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in-the-blank: the answer followed by 'with' is an idiom for agreeing with or backing.
explanation.definitionFit: To go along with someone is to agree with or back them, a phrasal verb completed by the answer.

clue.text: Drake's boat could be adapted for youth transport

indicators.note: something adapted is altered into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Francis Drake's ship might be refitted to carry young people.
explanation.walkthrough: Drake is the Elizabethan sea captain, which steers thoughts toward the Golden Hind.
explanation.definitionFit: A skateboard is a wheeled board ridden mainly by teenagers, so a young person's way of getting around.

clue.text: Trouble after a small case of fruit

indicators.note: one part following another is placed after it in the answer

blocks.note: a grammatical case, the vocative, shortened

explanation.surface: Bother follows the arrival of a little crate of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Small means abbreviated: VOC stands for the vocative case of Latin grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: The avocado is the pear-shaped tropical fruit with green flesh and a large stone.

clue.text: Father's relative has his name in stone

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is put inside it

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A dad's kinsman has his name carved on a gravestone.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnate is a kinsman descended through the male line, related on the father's side.

clue.text: Old time coppers?

blocks.note: surface reading: police officers from days gone by
setter's reading: police walk a beat, so a past era of beat bobbies names a 1950s literary movement

explanation.walkthrough: Coppers are British police, who patrol a beat; the answer is the American writers' movement of Kerouac and Ginsberg.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beat Generation was the 1950s group of American writers, a cohort now long past.

clue.text: Prophet sounds dry and withered

indicators.note: sounds signals that the word is identified by how it is spoken rather than spelt

explanation.surface: An old prophet's voice is parched and his body shrivelled.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer is one who sees into the future, a visionary or prophet.

clue.text: One sample carries exceptional load of sin

indicators.note: exceptional means out of the ordinary, so the word after it is not in its usual order
something that carries another holds it within

explanation.surface: A single specimen bears an extraordinary burden of wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One sample' is a single charade that does the carrying: the scrambled word sits between its two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Idolatry, worshipping false gods, is condemned in the Commandments as a grave sin.

clue.text: Memory recalled drink - spirit

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word runs back to front

explanation.surface: Remembering a drink lifts the spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Morale is the confidence and spirit of a person or group, as in team spirit.

clue.text: Discernment of age trouble with shelter to the old

indicators.note: something troubled is stirred up, so these letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: the sheltered side away from the wind
an archaic spelling of the, as in Ye Olde Shoppe

explanation.surface: Perceptiveness lessens with the troubles of ageing, though elderly people need protection.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle eye is unusually keen sight or watchfulness, so sharp perception or discernment.

clue.text: How a Cockney says he works with this

definitions.text: How a Cockney says he works with this

blocks.note: surface reading: a question of East End accent
setter's reading: a Cockney who works harder, with the h dropped, sounds as if he works with zeal

explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop their h's and their r's, so 'he works harder' comes out sounding like the answer. A Cockney is a working-class Londoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardour is passion or keen enthusiasm, the zeal with which a keen worker goes about his job.
